title: Labor induction and social media influence: An analytical video-based cross-sectional study to assess quality, reliability, and accuracy of related content on TikTok
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study with no reported share of items classified false/inaccurate. The Methods define a three-level misinformation categorisation (“information with over 50 % misinformation was labeled as ‘inaccurate or misinformative’; videos with under 50 % but above 25 % misinformation were considered as ‘partially accurate’; videos with under 25 % misinformation were defined as ‘accurate and evidence-based’”), but the Results NEVER report that distribution — no count or percentage of the 150 videos falling in any misinformation category appears anywhere in the paper. Everything reported is a MEDIAN of a quality/reliability instrument (PEMAT A/V understandability and actionability, VIQI including its “Information accuracy” subscale, mDISCERN, GQS), stratified by creator type. Per §3, a Likert accuracy scale reported only as a median/mean is not a share and yields no row; per §1 a quality-only study is excluded. The only shares reported are creator-type composition (patients 52 % (78/150), healthcare 39 % (59/150), other 9 % (13/150)), which is not a misinformation numerator.
missed_or_uncertain: Seen but not extractable: (1) VIQI “Information accuracy” medians — healthcare 4.00 [4.00, 4.00], other 4.00 [3.00, 4.00], patients 2.50 [2.00, 3.00], p < 0.001 — an accuracy scale reported as medians only, no share of videos above any threshold, so no row (§3). (2) GQS medians (healthcare 4.00, other 4.00, patients 2.50) with the stated threshold “Videos graded three and above by GQS were considered of high-quality information” — the threshold is defined but the share of videos meeting it is never reported. (3) mDISCERN medians (2.00 in all three groups) and PEMAT understandability/actionability medians — quality/reliability instruments, medians only. (4) Creator-type shares (52 % patients, 39 % healthcare, 9 % other of 150) — composition, not falsity. ADJUDICATOR NOTE: had the misinformation distribution been reported it would have been a CONTENT row (fact-checking against WHO/obstetric IOL guidelines by two gynaecologists with a senior adjudicator, TikTok, global/English-only, topic health_other, denom_scope topical with denom_selection=curated because only the top 150 of 482 videos ranked by platform visibility were analysed, sampling_frame keyword_topical, ground_truth researcher_coding, n = 150 videos, date 13 January 2025). The paper's own limitations section concedes “the lack of an official inter-rater reliability evaluation”. If the first extractor recorded a prevalence value for this paper, it is likely to be either the creator-type composition or a value read from Fig. 1's flow chart rather than a reported misinformation share; the text file contains no such number.

rob.design: Cross-sectional TikTok content analysis, single time point (13 January 2025). Search query “Induction of Labor” / #inductionoflabor from a newly created account to avoid personalisation; 482 videos identified, the top 150 ranked by platform visibility and meeting inclusion criteria analysed (English or audio-free, IOL as primary topic, duplicates excluded). Two authors (A.D.P., C.F.) screened; two gynaecologists (R.M., A.C.) independently scored each video against WHO recommendations and obstetric guidelines, with a senior gynaecologist (G.S., >500 IOL procedures) resolving disagreements by consensus. No inter-rater reliability statistic — explicitly acknowledged as a limitation (“the lack of an official inter-rater reliability evaluation ... use of consensus scoring may have masked variability”). Other limitations: single time point, English only, engagement metrics not analysed, reproducibility limited by TikTok's default ranking algorithm.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation level in the videos was categorized according to the following definitions: information with over 50 % misinformation was labeled as “ inaccurate or misinformative ” ; videos with under 50 % but above 25 % misinformation were considered as “ partially accurate ” ; videos with under 25 % misinformation were defined as “ accurate and evidence-based. ”
rob.item10_quote: One hundred fifty TikTok videos were examined. The contents were created mainly from patients 52 % (78/150), 39 % from healthcare (59/150), and 9 % (13/150) from other sources.
